newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ukraine promises victory for foreign investors.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine promises victory for foreign investors.

text.p: Foreign investors eager to know more about Ukraine at an investment conference were warned on Wednesday they would get a wild ride if they entered the market -- but would emerge as winners in the end.

"A Formula One driver in rainy conditions will think about whether to step on the gas or not. Here, no matter what you do, you will win," Serhiy Oxanytch, president of Kinto Investments and Securities, told entrepreneurs.

The "Investment Window for Ukraine" conference came at a delicate time for the former Soviet republic of 50 million people, after months of Western media reports focusing on an investment climate at best labelled as unwelcoming.

But top Ukrainian ministers attending the conference, along with German bankers and firms doing business in Ukraine or considering it, pointed to strides made in achieving economic stability in the six years since independence.

"Trade has increased, our new currency is stable and inflation this year will be under 20 percent and not 37 percent like last year," said Deputy Prime Minister Serhiy Tyhypko, who is responsible for reform. "Ukraine is in fact the world leader in slowed inflation."

Ukraine has attracted only $1.5 billion in direct foreign investment since it broke away from Moscow in 1991, and investors' most common complaints have been about high taxes, inconsistent and ever-changing laws, and demands for bribes.

But ministers homed in on the huge investment potential of Ukraine, the second largest country in Europe, whose impending privatisations of agriculture, industrial and energy sector enterprises are expected to boost nascent stock markets.

Tyhypko, appointed in April to replace Viktor Pynzenyk who quit in disgust over the slow pace of reforms, announced an issue of foreign bonds on the European market would follow Ukraine's debut of yen-denominated bonds in September.
"I believe Ukraine will solve its problems. We need more time and more work," he said.

Ukraine, whose inflation in 1993 reached 10,000 percent, is in talks this week with the International Monetary Fund over delivery of a three-year, $2.5 to $3 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) -- endangered by a nearly six-month delay in the 1997 budget. It was finally passed by parliament on June 27.

But President Leonid Kuchma said on Tuesday he was happy with the pace of reforms, and a top World Bank official said this week he was confident Ukraine could meet foreign borrowing targets in this year's deficit.

"There is a final destination, but we're not there yet. The direction is right," said Yuri Poluneyev, a European Bank for Reconstruction and Development director appointed by the Ukrainian government.

Potential investors at the conference had mixed reactions to the promises, made before by Ukraine, which spent its early post-independence years nation-building before Kuchma announced an economic reform programme in late 1994.
One German banker, who asked not to be named, said he was still nervous about bureaucratic hurdles despite assurances.
But Royal Dutch/Shell unit Shell International Gas announced hopes of investing $1.5 billion in Ukraine's existing gas pipelines.
Joost Sliphorst, general manager of the Netherlands' PTT Telecom which has invested in several ventures in Ukraine, said facing investment problems had paid off.

"There is a jungle of legislation, licences, and I could go for another conference about taxes. But we face them and we solve them every day," Sliphorst said. "It is possible to start a safe, solid, profitable business in Ukraine."
